Listen, I understand the sentiment because of the way the humanities have taken such a hit in the last couple decades. But this just isn't true. Well, there are degrees of truth to what you are saying, but you're misrepresenting psychology undoubtedly.

Psychology is not a core science. There isn't anyone claiming that it is. Examples of core sciences are physics, chemistry (including biochem and phys chem), biology, astronomy/cosmology, genetics and molecular biology, neuroscience, etc.

The reason psychology is not a core science is because fundamentally we haven't solved the mind-body problem. Psychology is walking a borderland between material and the immaterial (ostensibly) because we haven't discovered what consciousness is. This was realized many many decades ago, and psychology as a whole basically said, "To hell with it." Then you had the identity correspondence theories arise which basically said: every mental state corresponds to a physical state. We don't know how or why, but we know they do. Consciousness is a barrier that science may never break, aka an insoluble problem, so we aren't going to deal with it at all.

The problem of consciousness got shoved out of psychology and moved where everything like this gets moved: philosophy.

Psychology for nearly a century has operated on the correspondence basis and has taken really what is a functionalist perspective, which is to say that a brain state X that corresponds with a particular behavioral output literally IS the mental state Y. So it became about identifying behavioral outputs and identifying them with brain states and the regions in which they occur. As an example, a feeling of love or rage literally IS the associated dynamic neural pattern that accompanies it. No further attempts are being made in psychology to go beyond this. At this point, that is for philosophy.

Insofar as psychology is attempting to develop theories about behavior and some of its physical correlates or categorical correlates, it is a science. An attempt to categorize and describe behavioral observations about the lived experience of being something is worthwhile. Tying behavioral output to psychological states is a useful endeavor. But it is still not as physicalist as neuroscience. Feverishly attempting to divert attention away from this fact: psychology is still dealing in the subjective world, just on the low key.

Since we are dealing with an unsolved problem, one which is essentially philosophical, it is vulnerable to infiltration politically. Whenever there is a philosophical swamp to fall into, the issue often becomes moral at the level of society. So moral politics is now a part of psychology. I think one of it's biggest issues is that it cannot make up it's mind essentially. If it becomes completely physicalist, there is no difference between it and cognitive neuroscience. If it tries to put forward a theory on consciousness, it is right back where it was a little over a century ago when it gave up. It's issue is that it is noncommittal at this point. It's stuck in the mud. It is true that I don't think much has been done in the area of psychology that is worth reading in the last 20 years.
What do you think it world take to pull itself out of the mud again?

(1) Stop trying so fucking hard to legitimize itself as a "science". Form a more cohesive philosophy about what science is and what the limitations of empirical science are with respect to the human mind. Stop trying to fit into a mold, and start exploring what is demanding to be answered, but which is currently being ignored because it's not 'scientific'.

(2) Develop a better theory that can reconcile the neuroscience with the subjective experience.

It ultimately needs to develop it's own identity because it is quickly being cannibalized by cognitive neuroscience and philosophy. If you're going to operate on the framework that mental states ARE physical brain states, then a harder empirical science like neuro is going to overtake you. Psychology's only saving grace at this point is that neuro isn't as interested in describing global behavioral patterns as it is with describing the physical correlates of the behavior, and at this stage that refers to relatively simpler behaviors, i.e. not whole human personality. Neuro isn't really interested in what a gender experience is like, as an example.

In the areas where psychology is trying to make empirical connections, it's shooting itself in the foot. Let's think about what modern psychology is really about: intelligence description and assessment, personality theory and assessment, and behavioral modification toward better adaptation to the demands of life.

They look at human decision making, the outcomes of those decisions, and try to piece together why people make their decisions based on their personality types, who is getting the best outcomes, and then how to help someone struggling to behave in ways more typical of those having better outcomes.

But in trying so hard to be a "core science" they ignore the most important part of human decision making: meaning or our subjective judgments about the valence/significance of things. That implies values. Which imply morals. So when psychologists start trying to talk about their observations, perhaps that having a certain quality or acting a certain way is what explains why certain subsets of people have the outcomes they do, there are implicit value assumptions being made. Post-modernism doesn't like this. It actively fights against any kind of meta-narrative to the human experience, and so it fights the psychological theories that might explain why certain people tend to be happier, or more successful, or why there are discrepancies between groups on the basis of IQ, personality, and behavior. If you want "scientific" explanations for these you are forced to start categorizing people, and the modern political climate is trying to do away with these categorizations.

Psychology is caving and de-legitimizing itself because it isn't telling the truth. It has run into conclusions that it can't move forward with, because at the end of the psychological road comes value claims. People wanting to succeed in the field are getting indoctrinated beginning in undergrad (and it's reinforced all the way up the chain), so there is also the reality we are training bad psychologists now too. But this also means we have to recognize how the field is influenced by the job markets. If you take this road - clinical psych for example - you have two options: practice or teach/research. Many people get into psych to do research, and there is an immense pressure to conform if you want to remain in academia and get a tenure-track position. Making the right professional network connections and getting into the right labs all require a great deal of social navigating, and when the field has been compromised, the pressures start working against good psychology.

So if psychology wants to continue down this road, it has to start telling the truth, or it needs to find a new way to approach exploring new territory, currently deemed pseudo-scientific or parapsychological phenomenon. The results of research in these fringe areas could help open the door to a better theory of human consciousness and broaden the subject into more areas than only philosophy of mind.

One major difficulty is that we tend to look at human psychology as relatively stable across long time tables. But psychology has evolved as human organization has evolved. A good example would be the big 5 personality index. There is a pretty large body of research to back this formulation of personality, a lot of which has been replicated. The caveat, almost nothing in psychology is universal. For example, there was a study where the big 5 was assessed with the Tsimane (a South American tribe of hunter gatherers), and it didn't fit. Why? Because their social organization is simpler, with only a few "tracks" to take in life: hunter, gatherer, shaman. I find it difficult to say that the way psychology has approached describing personality theory is not scientific because it is not universal. Again, we are throwing the subjective component of the human mind into this. It isn't physics. Having the unity of physics is impossible in studying the human mind. That said, I agree with you that a lot of psychology is bunk, or at least vastly oversimplified.

So maybe it's that our definitions of "science" are different. I tend to take something as a science based on its approach and its philosophy. Is it trying to carefully observe, gather a great deal of data, make careful hypothesis and test them empirically? Is it's approach inclusive to the evidence that is presenting itself, or does it ignore observations to sustain a pet theory? To me this is a science.

A stricter view of science probably comes down to methodology. Not only does the theory have to explain the observations that have been made, but it needs to explain all of the observations that are to be made. It needs to be quantitative for the most part, because part of the "scientific" view of the universe is as a UNITY, whereby if one element of the universe can be explained mathematically, then all elements of that universe should be explainable mathematically. Moreover, a single study should be reproducible using precisely the same methods.

Again, it is tough for psychology to fit that mold. But I think it's fair to say psychology approaches what is a hybrid of material-immaterial phenomena with, at the very least, as scientific a philosophy as you can. In fact, I think it's one thing that has held it back to be honest.

I'm about halfway through David Chalmer's "The Conscious Mind" right now. I'm terribly interested in consciousness, but it's interesting how history and current theory plays a directing role in the way we approach theories about consciousness. Chalmer's book is a serious philosophical work, and so far I appreciate it. He is at least - as far as I can tell - attempting to refute a completely materialist explanation of consciousness.

But at the same time, he introduces supervenience as a concept to explain how many of the "psychological" (as opposed to experiential) aspects of consciousness still supervene on physical principles. What I am getting so far is that he is stripping all of the real agency/action/intention away from consciousness (and giving that over to deterministic physicalism), and leaving what's left over as "consciousness" in the phenomenal sense.

It makes it seem like our conscious experience is really this unimportant, ineffectual sort of thing that is basically just "the qualitative experience had in the theater of the mind". It isn't material, but also doesn't really have anything to do with what the mind does in the universe or in our lives. Belief, desire, intentions may have some "tinge" of experience to them, but they aren't really conscious experiences. He's kind of like a functionalist walking around in non-reductionist clothing.
